items.name: Readability
items.evidence: No comment explains the `# /*` / `'''` / `# */` language switch. Names in the bigint logic are cryptic (`a`, `b`, `c`, `tmp`, `len_a`), and so are the constants `1000000000ULL` and `(n / 20) + 10`. The layout is otherwise tidy.

items.name: Maintainability
items.evidence: fib_c is about 60 lines and does allocation, base-10^9 bigint addition and printing in one function. The arbitrary-precision engine is more machinery than the task needs, and base cases are handled separately in C and Python.

items.name: Robustness
items.evidence: No input validation in C: `atoi(argv[1])`, and a missing argument quietly computes f(0) and exits 0. If calloc fails, it frees and returns, printing nothing and exiting 0, so the error is swallowed. Negative input prints 0 in both languages. Magic constants repeat.

items.name: Boundary and large inputs
items.evidence: f(0), f(1), f(90), f(1000) and f(10000) match across both languages, both iterative. Argument errors are not handled: a missing argument gives `n = 0` and exit 0, a negative n prints 0, and C `atoi("abc")` prints 0. Only Python's int() fails on non-numeric input.

items.name: Exact invocation contract
items.evidence: Works with exactly the two given commands. Compiles cleanly even with `-Wall -Wextra -Werror`, and each run prints only the number (e.g. `55`).
